name: DVWA: Command Injection to Shell
short_description: Exploit command injection in DVWA to get a reverse shell on the web server.
description: DVWA (Damn Vulnerable Web Application) has a command injection vulnerability in the 'ping' functionality. We'll exploit this to execute arbitrary commands and get a reverse shell. This teaches OS command injection - OWASP Top 10 #1.
handler_message:
Cerberus maintains a public-facing customer portal at 172.20.0.10. Behind the corporate facade, the application is riddled with vulnerabilities.

The development team prioritized features over security. Command injection in the network diagnostics page. Classic mistake.

But here's what matters: the portal's database contains customer records. And those customers don't match any legitimate business. Shell companies. Fronts. The money laundering infrastructure that keeps NIGHTFALL funded.

Get a shell. Then we dig into their data.
episode_intro:
The false flag evidence is damning. But evidence doesn't explain motive.

Why would anyone engineer a massive infrastructure attack on their own country? Who benefits when power grids fail and water systems go offline?

Follow the money. That's the answer. Somewhere in Cerberus's systems is the financial trail - the contracts, the shell companies, the offshore accounts that make NIGHTFALL profitable.

The customer portal is the first thread. A web application with more holes than security. Command injection in the ping function. Amateur hour.

But behind the sloppy code is a database full of transactions. Customers who don't exist. Payments for services never rendered.

Time to see who's been paying for the end of the world.
episode_outro:
The shell gives you access. And the access reveals the truth.

The customer database is a fiction. Company names that sound real but have no presence. Addresses that map to empty lots. Bank accounts that route through a maze of offshore entities.

But the money is very real. Millions flowing into Cerberus from sources that don't exist. Payments for 'infrastructure consulting' that never happened.

You find references to a 'primary investor' - no name, just a code: PROMETHEUS. The largest deposits trace back to accounts in Cyprus, the Caymans, and Singapore.

Whoever PROMETHEUS is, they're funding NIGHTFALL. And the database behind this portal might have more details.

SQL injection is the next step. Bypass the application layer. Talk directly to the data.

interstitial.title: Episode 6: INPUT VALIDATION
interstitial.content:
PREVIOUSLY: The build farm revealed Cerberus's false flag strategy. Chinese strings. Beijing IP addresses. Compilation timestamps from the wrong timezone.

They're not just planning an attack - they're manufacturing evidence to blame another nation.

But evidence doesn't explain motive. Why would an American company engineer an attack on American infrastructure?

Follow the money. Cerberus's customer portal at 172.20.0.10 handles financial transactions. And the development team left command injection vulnerabilities in the network diagnostics page.

Get a shell. Find the money trail. Understand who profits when NIGHTFALL goes live.

steps.title: Open DVWA in browser
steps.narrative: The Cerberus customer portal runs on DVWA - a deliberately vulnerable web application. In the real world, this represents any poorly-secured web application. Open http://localhost:8080 and login with admin/password. Set security to 'Low' to simulate a system with no input validation.

steps.title: Navigate to Command Injection
steps.narrative: The network diagnostics page accepts an IP address for a ping test. Classic functionality on corporate portals. But the developers trusted user input - fatal mistake. The application doesn't sanitize what you type. Find 'Command Injection' in the left menu.

steps.title: Test command injection
steps.narrative: The semicolon terminates the ping command. Everything after it executes as a new command. 'id' shows the current user. If you see www-data's information after the ping results, the injection works. The application is trusting your input and executing it.

steps.title: Set up a listener in Kali
steps.narrative: Before sending a reverse shell, you need something to catch it. Netcat in listen mode (-l) on port 4444, verbose (-v), no DNS lookups (-n), with port specification (-p). This terminal will wait for the incoming connection.

steps.title: Send reverse shell payload
steps.narrative: This is a bash reverse shell. It creates an interactive bash session (-i) and redirects all input/output to a TCP connection to your Kali machine. Enter this in the DVWA form. When you submit, check your Netcat terminal - a shell should connect.

steps.title: Verify shell access
steps.narrative: In your Netcat terminal: no prompt appears, but you have a shell. Type 'id' and press Enter. You're www-data - the web server user. Limited privileges, but enough to explore the application and its data.

steps.title: Check hostname
steps.narrative: Confirm you're on the Cerberus portal server. Every compromised system is a pivot point - potential access to internal networks, databases, and other systems that the public-facing server can reach.

steps.title: Upgrade to interactive shell
steps.narrative: Spawn a proper terminal. Raw reverse shells are functional but awkward. Python's pty module gives you command history, tab completion, and proper signal handling. Much more comfortable for extended exploration.

steps.title: Explore the web root
steps.narrative: The web root contains the application code. Configuration files often include database credentials, API keys, and other secrets that developers shouldn't have committed. Look for config.php, .env files, anything that might contain credentials.

steps.title: Read database config
steps.narrative: Database credentials. Username, password, host, database name. This is how web applications store connection information - often in plaintext in config files. With these credentials, you can access the database directly and bypass application-level controls.

success_criteria: You have a shell on the Cerberus portal server. Database credentials are exposed. You can explore the application and prepare for SQL injection attacks.
next_steps: Extract user data: SELECT * FROM users;
